why_use_this: The compiler's own builtin `Graph` type already covers single-source shortest path (`graph_dijkstra`), MST (`graph_mst_kruskal`/`_prim`), BFS/DFS reachability, and topological sort -- reach for THIS package only when you need something beyond that fixed set, because the builtin `Graph` is opaque from vāṇी source (no way to enumerate a node's neighbors or list edges), so nothing beyond the compiler's own algorithm list can be built on top of it. This package uses its own flat adjacency-matrix encoding instead, specifically to support all-pairs shortest path (Floyd-Warshall), strongly-connected components (Kosaraju), max-flow/min-cut (Edmonds-Karp), bipartite matching (Kuhn's / Hopcroft-Karp), and graph coloring -- none of which the builtin type can express. It also covers combinatorics (permutation/combination enumeration, integer-partition counting) that has nothing to do with graphs at all, just grouped here as "discrete math" generally. Every algorithm here is the simplest textbook-correct choice, not the asymptotically optimal one (Floyd-Warshall not Johnson's, Kosaraju not Tarjan) -- see the README's "Scope decisions" if you specifically need the faster asymptotic complexity for a large graph.

math_notes.disc_floyd_warshall: The all-pairs shortest-path dynamic-programming recurrence: for each intermediate node \( k = 0, \ldots, n-1 \) in turn, \( \text{dist}[i][j] \leftarrow \min\big(\text{dist}[i][j],\ \text{dist}[i][k] + \text{dist}[k][j]\big) \) for every pair \( (i,j) \) -- after all \( n \) values of \( k \) have been processed, \( \text{dist}[i][j] \) holds the true shortest-path distance from \( i \) to \( j \) allowing any intermediate nodes, in \( O(n^3) \).
math_notes.disc_max_flow: Edmonds-Karp: repeatedly find an augmenting path from source to sink in the residual graph via BFS (guaranteeing the shortest such path each time, which is what bounds this at \( O(VE^2) \) rather than being merely correct-but-unbounded like generic Ford-Fulkerson), push the minimum residual capacity along that path, and repeat until no augmenting path remains. The returned flow value provably equals the capacity of the minimum cut separating source from sink (the max-flow-min-cut theorem) -- this package's own tests verify that equality directly against `disc_min_cut_nodes`'s output rather than assuming the theorem holds.
math_notes.disc_min_cut_nodes: After `disc_max_flow` saturates the network, the set of nodes still reachable from `source` in the residual graph (via BFS) is exactly one side of a minimum cut -- every edge crossing from this reachable set to its complement is a saturated edge whose combined capacity equals the max-flow value (the max-flow-min-cut theorem).
math_notes.disc_partition_count: Computes \( p(n) \), the integer partition function (the number of ways to write \( n \) as a sum of positive integers, order not mattering) -- via the unbounded-knapsack-style DP \( \text{dp}[i] \mathrel{+}= \text{dp}[i-k] \) for each allowed part size \( k = 1, \ldots, n \) in turn, the same recurrence that falls out of expanding the generating function \( \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{1-x^k} \) and reading off the coefficient of \( x^n \).
